checks.claim: Key: a Chihuahua and a Great Dane are one species (all dog breeds are one species, Canis lupus familiaris, and cross-breeds are fertile)
checks.note: Grokipedia classes the dog as a subspecies of the grey wolf (Canis lupus familiaris); all breeds are that one taxon and cross-breeds (e.g. Labradoodles) breed. A Chihuahua and a Great Dane may struggle to mate naturally for size, but their genes are compatible and the stem's test ('can mate and have young that have young') is met in principle. Fine at grade 6.

checks.claim: Context: a Chihuahua under 3 kg, a Great Dane over 70 kg; more size variation than any other land mammal (grade note)
checks.note: Grokipedia Dog: 'from Chihuahuas under 3 kg to Great Danes over 70 kg' and variation 'surpassing body size variation in any other terrestrial mammal'. Grokipedia Great Dane gives males 63-79 kg, so 'over 70' is a big male, not every Dane; acceptable as an illustration of the extremes.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: a Shire horse and a donkey (mule almost never able to breed)
checks.note: Mules are 'almost universally sterile' (about 99%); horse 64, donkey 62, mule 63 chromosomes; only some 60 fertile female mules recorded. 'Almost never' is exactly right. A Shire is a horse breed, so the pair is horse x donkey. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: a rabbit and a hare (do not interbreed)
checks.note: Modern sources agree rabbits and hares cannot produce hybrids (hares 48 chromosomes, rabbits 44; different genera). Only 19th-century anecdotes claim otherwise. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: an alligator and a crocodile (different families)
checks.note: Alligators are Alligatoridae, true crocodiles Crocodylidae. No hybrids known. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Key: whether a student tastes PTC is set by the genes he or she inherited
checks.note: TAS2R38 accounts for '50-80% of the phenotypic variance'; PTC paper is a 'standard tool for demonstrating Mendelian genetics'. Of the four choices the inherited genes is plainly the cause. geneticmyths.com notes other genes and age play a smaller part, which does not threaten the key.

checks.claim: Context: 'Whether a person tastes PTC depends on a gene called TAS2R38, passed down from parents'
checks.note: True: 'One gene (TAS2R38) does have a major effect'. It is not the only factor (other genes, age), but 'depends on' is not 'depends only on', so the simplification holds.

checks.claim: Stem and context: about three in four taste it bitter; 'about one person in four tastes no bitterness at all'
checks.note: Grokipedia gives nontasters as about 25%. NIDCD: 27-28% in people of European origin, 10-16% in most African, Asian and Native American groups, about 50% in Australian Aborigines. One in four is a fair round figure for a typical Western class; optional polish: 'in many groups, about one person in four'. Paper-strip nontasters typically report no taste, though some taste very strong solutions; fine at strip strength.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the part of the tongue the strip touched (tongue map is a myth); context 'taste buds all over the tongue can sense bitterness'
checks.note: The tongue map is 'scientifically discredited'; all tastes are detected across the tongue. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: how long the strip was held; what was eaten for breakfast
checks.note: Neither explains a taster/nontaster split; nontasters do not detect PTC at strip strength however long they hold it. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Key: the soil in the friend's garden changed the colour (bigleaf hydrangea blue in acid soil with aluminium, pink in alkaline)
checks.note: Grokipedia: blue below about pH 5.5, where Al3+ 'is taken up by the plant roots'; pink above 6.5, where aluminium precipitates 'preventing uptake'. Georgia Extension agrees (fieldreport.caes.uga.edu/publications/C973/). A blue-flowered bush must be a colour-changing kind (white cultivars do not change), so the stem is consistent.

checks.claim: Context: 'A cutting grows into a plant with the same genes as the bush it came from'
checks.note: Cuttings produce genetically identical clones.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: Sunlight in the friend's garden
checks.note: Truly wrong. Grokipedia says intense sun, heat and age only fade the pigment as a bloom ages; light does not switch a hue from blue to pink. Extension sources (UGA, UMass, NC State) name soil pH and aluminium as the cause and never light.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: a change in the cutting's genes; pollen from the friend's other flowers
checks.note: A cutting is a clone ('genetically identical clones without such recombination', Grokipedia Cutting (plant)), so a gene change is not the likely cause. The showy mophead blooms are 'showy, sterile florets', and Grokipedia ties colour only to soil pH, aluminium and pigment chemistry, never to pollination. Both truly wrong.

checks.claim: Key: sowing the biggest beans from a line of identical genes gives beans of the usual size (Johannsen's pure lines)
checks.note: Johannsen sowed the heaviest and lightest seeds within pure lines of the self-pollinating Princess bean; selection 'produced no lasting heritable shifts' and offspring means stayed stable. Hamburg Botany Online agrees: he 'chose the lightest and the heaviest seeds of the phenotype-variations of pure lines ... without achieving a change of the average seed weight'.

checks.claim: Context: Wilhelm Johannsen, the botanist who coined the word gene
checks.note: Danish botanist and geneticist (professor of plant physiology, Copenhagen); coined 'gene' in 1909 in Elemente der exakten Erblichkeitslehre.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: as big as the sown beans; even bigger; smaller than usual
checks.note: 'A selection within pure lines is thus without effect': large and small parent seeds gave progeny with the line's usual mean; none of the three alternatives fits. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Key: more brown beetles live to pass their colour on (Berkeley's green/brown beetle model)
checks.note: Berkeley: green beetles 'tend to get eaten by birds and survive to reproduce less often than brown beetles do'; survivors 'have offspring of the same color because this trait has a genetic basis'. Matches stem, key and context.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: green beetles turn brown to hide; green parents have brown young to keep them safe; the soil stains them
checks.note: The change 'does not involve effort, trying, or wanting' and 'cannot sense what a species or an individual' needs; in the model no beetle changes colour. All three are the standard misconceptions and truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: no beetle changes colour to suit the soil; parents cannot give young a colour because the young need it
checks.note: True within the model the stem sets up.

checks.claim: Stem: biologists had just finished measuring the small lizards on two islands when two hurricanes struck in 2017; returned weeks later; survivors had bigger toe pads on average
checks.note: Donihue et al., Nature 560:88-91 (2018): Anolis scriptus on Pine Cay and Water Cay, Turks and Caicos, measured just before Irma (landfall 8 Sept 2017), Maria followed (22 Sept); resurveyed about six weeks later; survivors had larger toe pads on fore- and hindlimbs, longer forelimbs, shorter femurs, smaller bodies (abstract via digitalcommons.uri.edu/bio_facpubs/411). All stem details right.

checks.claim: Key: 'Lizards with bigger pads held on and lived' as the best explanation
checks.note: Matches the authors' own framing: Losos, 'hurricane-induced natural selection seems like the best explanation for these findings'. The stem's 'best explains' is suitably cautious.

checks.claim: Context: 'The storms changed no lizard's feet. Lizards that already had bigger toe pads held on to the branches in the wind while others lost their grip'
checks.note: Stated more firmly than the authors did. Nobody saw lizards lose their grip in the storm; the grip story comes from a later wind test on survivors (hindlimbs lost hold first). Losos named alternatives, including lizards blown in from another island and clinging lengthening the legs: 'We can't rule these possibilities out because this study was the result of serendipity.' The 2019 offspring result (below) argues against the storm reshaping feet, but the context should hedge. Fix: 'Most likely the storms changed no lizard's feet: lizards that already had bigger toe pads could hold on better in the wind, while others lost their grip.'

checks.claim: Context: 'the survivors were smaller on average, so the biggest lizards did not do best' (and wrong choice 'The biggest, strongest lizards were the ones that lived')
checks.note: Survivors had smaller body size, significant at both islands. Wrong choice truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: 'A year later, the survivors' young had toe pads just as big'
checks.note: Donihue et al., PNAS 117:10429 (2020): 'We repeated those surveys 18 mo (April 1 to 8, 2019) after our initial posthurricane survey', about a year and a half after the storms; young were small lizards judged by growth models to have hatched after April 2018, and their toe pads did not differ from the survivors'. (The WashU 2020 release says 'one year later', but the paper says 18 months.) Fix: 'A year and a half later, young lizards hatched after the storms had toe pads just as big.'

checks.claim: Wrong choices: clinging stretched each lizard's pads; the lizards grew bigger pads to grip
checks.note: Not the best explanation: the shift appeared within six weeks and persisted in young that never met the storm ('a transgenerational effect of extreme selection on toepad area'). Acceptable as wrong for a 'best explains' stem; note Losos did list stretching of the legs (not pads) as a possibility he could not rule out, which is why the stem must keep 'best'.

checks.claim: Key: when small, soft seeds dominate, the thin-beaked birds do best
checks.note: Zimmer on the Grants' Daphne Major finches: after the 1983 El Niño rains 'triggered a frenzy of small-seed plant growth', small-beaked ground finches ate the new seeds more efficiently and had more offspring. Gibbs and Grant, Nature 327:511 (1987), 'Oscillating selection on Darwin's finches': 'a reversal in the direction of selection following the opposite climatic extreme', tied to the food supply.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: thick-beaked; medium-beaked; thick and thin alike
checks.note: Selection ran against large beaks, not toward the middle. One subtlety: during the wet years themselves food was so plentiful that all ground finches bred repeatedly; the small-beaked edge showed most when food grew short again (1984-86), with mostly small seeds left. 'Alike' is therefore weakly defensible only for the boom years; the stem's 'do best' and the context's 'within a few years' keep the key right. Optional polish: 'Then years of heavy rain leave the island covered in small, soft seeds, and few big ones. When food runs short again, which birds do best?'

checks.claim: Context: a drought in 1977 favoured big beaks on a Galapagos island
checks.note: The 1977 drought 'left only large, hard seeds'; deeper-beaked finches survived far better; offspring beak depth rose 4-5% (Grokipedia); Zimmer: average beak 4% bigger within a few generations. Island is Daphne Major.

checks.claim: Context: after heavy rains in 1983 brought a flush of small seeds, the average beak shrank again within a few years
checks.note: Zimmer: 'the average beak shrank by 2.5% within a few years'. A 1993 Nature commentary (Nature 362:699, on Grant and Grant, Proc. R. Soc. B 251:111) reports small, soft seeds rising tenfold after the 1982-83 El Niño, the shift lasting to at least 1991, and a measured fall in G. fortis bill size close to the predicted one (search-result summary; page behind a login).

checks.claim: Context: a thinner beak eats small seeds more efficiently
checks.note: As stated by Zimmer and the Grants' foraging work.

checks.claim: Stem: swallows build mud nests under road bridges; cars kill some; biologists collected the dead for thirty years; the dead had longer wings on average than the living
checks.note: Charles Brown and Mary Bomberger Brown, Current Biology 23:R233 (2013): cliff swallows in southwest Nebraska nest under bridges and overpasses; 30-year study; road-killed birds 'disproportionately' longer-winged, compared with birds caught in mist nets. Science News: wings 'a few millimeters longer'.

checks.claim: Key: on average the wings have grown shorter
checks.note: The population's average wing length showed a significant long-term decline over the study, while road-killed birds' wings did not (Current Biology abstract via search; Science News 'average wing length ... has shrunk'). Wrong choices (longer; same; each bird's wings shrink with age) are truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: a shorter wing lets a swallow fly up and turn away from a car more quickly
checks.note: The authors' explanation: shorter wings let birds 'fly upward and pivot away from oncoming traffic'; Brown compares them to quail launching almost straight up. It is their proposed mechanism; acceptable at grade 6, and the context's last clause carries the caveat.

checks.claim: Context: far fewer died on the road; biologists say other causes may play a part
checks.note: Road kills fell from about 20 in 1982 to 4 in 2012 (Christian Science Monitor; Science News: only four in 2012) while the colonies grew. Brown says factors other than wing length may be involved (e.g. cars removing bolder birds); the team ruled out vehicle types, fewer birds and more scavengers. The caveat is stated as cautiously as the authors did.

checks.claim: Stem: a fungus has been killing ash trees across Europe; in some woods most have died (ash dieback)
checks.note: Hymenoscyphus fraxineus, native to East Asia, reached Europe in the early 1990s and now covers nearly all of it; surveys show 'up to 70% tree death in woodlands and 85% in plantations'. QMUL gives 69% woodlands / 85% plantations as the highest. 'In some woods most' is right.

checks.claim: Key: seedlings of the healthy trees can inherit resistance
checks.note: QMUL (Buggs): 'resistance to ash is heritable and will respond well to natural selection'.

checks.claim: Context: in one English wood the new generation was found more resistant, on average, than the old trees
checks.note: Metheringham et al., Science 388:1422 (26 June 2025), Marden Park wood, Surrey (Woodland Trust): juveniles established after the epidemic had higher genomically estimated breeding values for resistance than pre-epidemic adults. The finding is from DNA (thousands of small-effect variants), not from watching the trees resist; the release says the young generation 'appears more resistant'. True as a summary. Optional precision: 'scientists found the young trees carry more of the genes for resistance than the old trees around them.'

checks.claim: Context: young ash trees without resistance die fastest of all (and wrong choice 'Young trees are too small for the fungus to harm')
checks.note: RHS: 'Young trees can be killed in one season' while older trees 'tend to succumb after several seasons'. Grokipedia: 'killing up to 90% of young ash trees'. Wrong choice truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: sick trees catch resistance from healthy ones; dying trees grow resistance before they die
checks.note: Resistance is inherited through genes and is polygenic; it does not spread between trees or appear on demand. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Stem: 'a soil fungus called Panama disease'
checks.note: Panama disease is the name of the disease, not of the fungus: 'Panama disease, also known as Fusarium wilt, is a destructive soil-borne fungal disease', caused by the fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense. Wikipedia: 'a wilt caused by the fungus Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. cubense'. Fix: 'In the 1950s Panama disease, caused by a soil fungus, swept through its plantations...' (or 'a soil fungus that causes Panama disease').

checks.claim: Stem: Gros Michel once the main banana shipped to Europe and North America; in the 1950s the disease wiped out huge stretches of plantations in Central America
checks.note: 'once the dominant export banana to Europe and North America'; 'In the 1950s, Panama disease wiped out vast tracts of Gros Michel plantations in Central America'. Grokipedia Panama disease: Race 1 devastated Gros Michel 'in the 1950s and 1960s'.

checks.claim: Key: every plant was a copy of the same plant
checks.note: Grokipedia: Gros Michel's 'clonal uniformity enabled Foc race 1 to collapse export plantations in the Americas'; bananas are propagated vegetatively from suckers.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: bananas cannot fight off any fungus; the fungus kills every kind of plant; it killed each plant in a single day
checks.note: Cavendish shows 'strong resistance to TR1' (so bananas can resist); Foc has 'host specificity to Musa species'; a plant collapses 'within six to twelve months after initial symptoms'. All truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: bananas grown from shoots, not seeds; growers switched to the Cavendish, which resisted that fungus; every Cavendish is a copy too; a new strain now threatens it
checks.note: Cavendish is 'seedless and reproductively sterile', propagated from suckers (shoots) or tissue culture, giving 'genetically identical offspring'; exporters switched by the 1960s (Wikipedia); Cavendish resists Race 1 but Tropical Race 4 is 'an existential threat' (Grokipedia Panama disease). Note: the context itself correctly says the fungus causes the disease ('resisted that fungus'), so only the stem's wording needs the fix.

unit_notes: Two errors, both small wording fixes. (1) Lizards (6544f4dac6): the offspring resurvey was 18 months after the post-storm survey (April 2019, Donihue et al. PNAS 2020), not 'a year later'; the context also states the grip mechanism and 'the storms changed no lizard's feet' more firmly than Losos and Donihue did (they could not rule out migration or plasticity and called selection 'the best explanation'), so hedge it with 'most likely'. The stem's 'best explains' already matches their caution. (2) Gros Michel (ba26e95a16): Panama disease is the disease, not the fungus's name. Everything else checked out: Grants' 1977/1983 finch story is told right (selection after the 1983 rains bit as food grew short in 1984-86; the stem is fine); the swallows' caveat matches Brown's own; 'Sunlight' is truly wrong for the hydrangea (light only fades a bloom, it does not switch blue to pink); Johannsen's pure-line result is right; the PTC one-in-four figure fits European-origin groups (10-16% in most African, Asian and Native American groups), optional 'in many groups'.
